Article Title: Quote of the day by Sam Altman: “AI will probably most likely lead to the end of the world, but…” - strange reality of AI risk and business opportunity
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Sam Altman

“AI will probably most likely lead to the end of the world, but in the meantime, there'll be great companies.”

What does Sam Altman’s quote mean

Opportunities and risks behind the AI boom

What can be learned from the quote

New technology can create opportunity and uncertainty at the same time

Commercial success does not settle questions about safety

Powerful technologies require more than business thinking

Short-term gains can coexist with long-term concerns

The people building a technology can still recognise its risks

What the quote means for AI now

How to apply Sam Altman’s quote in your daily life

Look at both sides of a new opportunity. Before adopting a new app, tool or technology, consider what it can improve and what problems it might introduce.

Use technology without depending on it completely. AI can help with research, writing, planning and routine tasks, but important information should still be checked independently.

Think beyond immediate benefits. Saving time or money today may be useful, but it is worth considering how a decision could affect you later.

Separate success from safety. Something becoming popular or profitable does not automatically make it reliable or risk-free.

Stay adaptable. When technology changes the way work is done, learning how to use it can be more practical than simply resisting the change.

Question impressive claims. New technology can attract excitement and investment very quickly. Checking evidence before accepting claims helps avoid unnecessary risks.

Consider consequences for other people. A decision that is efficient for one person or business may create difficulties for employees, customers or the wider community.

Keep uncertainty in mind. Not every future consequence can be predicted. Recognising that uncertainty can lead to more careful decisions.

Artificial intelligence is being developed as a tool for productivity, research and business, yet the same technology has also prompted questions about risks that could extend far beyond the companies building it. OpenA CEO Sam Altman has spoken openly about this uneasy contrast. His comments capture a peculiar feature of the current AI boom: enormous commercial possibilities are emerging alongside concerns about where increasingly powerful systems could eventually lead. Rather than presenting these as separate conversations, Altman placed them together in one striking sentence, linking the possibility of serious consequences with the creation of successful companies along the way.The quote brings together two very different ideas. Altman is suggesting that artificial intelligence could eventually create risks on a scale far beyond an ordinary technological disruption. At the same time, he recognises that the period leading up to any such outcome could produce companies of extraordinary size and influence.The phrase “in the meantime” is doing much of the work. It points to the immediate commercial reality of AI rather than treating the technology only as a distant question about humanity’s future. Businesses are already being built around artificial intelligence, while established companies are incorporating AI into software, research, customer services, manufacturing and other areas.The comment therefore reflects a tension at the heart of the AI industry. The same technology can be viewed as a source of economic growth and as something that requires serious consideration of its potential risks.Technology has often created businesses that would have been difficult to imagine before the underlying innovation arrived. The internet produced search engines, online marketplaces, social networks and cloud-computing companies. Smartphones changed the economics of communication, advertising, transport and entertainment.AI is following a similar commercial pattern, although its potential applications are unusually broad. Companies can use models to generate text and images, analyse information, write software, assist researchers, automate routine work or provide specialised services. That has created opportunities for both established technology firms and smaller companies building products around AI capabilities.Altman’s wording is unusual because he does not separate this economic opportunity from the possibility of serious harm. The two ideas appear in the same sentence. That makes the quote less about predicting a particular future and more about acknowledging the strange position of the technology: businesses may flourish while society is still working out how powerful AI should become and how it should be controlled.A technology does not have to be entirely beneficial or entirely harmful. AI can create useful products while also introducing problems that businesses, governments and researchers have to address.A company can become successful without proving that every long-term consequence of its technology is understood. Financial performance and technological safety are different questions.AI development involves engineering and investment, but it also raises questions involving law, security, education, employment and public policy.The phrase “in the meantime” highlights how quickly commercial opportunities can emerge while broader consequences remain uncertain.Acknowledging potential danger does not necessarily mean rejecting the technology itself. Altman’s quote illustrates that distinction quite clearly.Artificial intelligence is no longer confined to research laboratories. Generative AI tools are being used for writing, coding, design, customer support, research and administrative work. Companies are also investing heavily in the infrastructure needed to train and operate increasingly capable models.That commercial expansion has made AI a significant business story in its own right. New firms are being created around specialised applications, while large technology companies are competing to develop their own models and AI services.At the same time, concerns surrounding the technology have become broader. Questions about inaccurate outputs, privacy, copyright, cybersecurity, employment and the misuse of AI have moved into mainstream discussions. More speculative concerns about highly advanced AI remain part of the debate as well.Altman’s quote fits into that wider picture because it does not treat economic growth and technological risk as mutually exclusive. Both can develop together.The quote can be applied to ordinary decisions by learning to look at both the opportunity and the risk involved. AI is a useful example, but the principle extends beyond technology.
Article Summary: OpenA CEO Sam Altman has spoken openly about this uneasy contrast. His comments capture a peculiar feature of the current AI boom. Businesses are already being built around artificial intelligence, while established companies are incorporating AI into software, research, customer services, manufacturing and other areas.

iPhone 18 Pro is the first iPhone with a variable aperture camera

Pro controls bring manual shutter speed and white balance to the Camera app

Apple Reference Image helps iPhone 18 Pro users prove what the camera saw

iPhone 18 Pro can add Cinematic mode effects after a video is shot

A20 Pro chip is built on 2nm and doubles AI processing power

A bigger vapour chamber keeps iPhone 18 Pro performance up for longer

iPhone 18 Pro Max battery lasts up to 43 hours of video playback in India

A smaller Dynamic Island shows three Live Activities at once

Siri AI arrives on iPhone 18 Pro with iOS 27

Apple has launched the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the most significant change sits inside the main camera. For the first time on an iPhone, the 48MP Fusion Main camera gets a variable aperture that physically controls how much light reaches the sensor. The new Pro models also get the 2nm A20 Pro chip, a larger vapour chamber, longer battery life, a smaller Dynamic Island and Siri AI, Apple's all-new assistant that arrives with iOS 27.The upgrades come at a higher price in India. The iPhone 18 Pro starts at Rs 1,64,900 and the iPhone 18 Pro Max at Rs 1,79,900, both Rs 30,000 more than the starting prices of last year's iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max. Storage still begins at 256GB, and the smaller Pro now gets a 2TB option too. Here are nine biggest features you need to know before you pre-order one tomorrow or even ordering one on September 18.iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max come in four storage variants, starting at 256GB. Here is what each one costs in India.Six laser-cut blades move the main camera between four apertures: f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8 and f/4.0. The camera switches automatically based on light and depth of field, or users can pick a setting themselves.At f/1.48, Apple claims around 50% better low-light performance and quicker Night mode shots. At f/4.0, more of the frame stays sharp, which helps with group photos. A new sensor sits behind the lens, and developers get an API to control the aperture in their own apps.Pro controls lets users customise the Camera app by pinning their most-used settings to the top. They can manually adjust aperture, shutter speed and white balance, with a histogram to check exposure. Photographic Styles 3 adds texture and grain controls to soften skin detail or add a film look, and these edits can be reversed later. The other rear cameras are 48MP too: a 13mm Ultra Wide and a Telephoto with 4x and 8x optical-quality zoom.In the new Reference mode, the main camera's sensor signs the pixel data as the photo is taken. Apple's Private Cloud Compute then develops it into a reference image that cannot be altered. This sits next to the regular photo in the Photos app, so users can compare the two and spot edits. The feature is opt-in and will not be available in China at launch. Apple also plans to add support for Google's SynthID standard, which identifies AI-generated or AI-edited images, later this year.Cinematic mode effects, which blur the background, can now be applied to regular videos after recording, including clips shot at up to 60fps. Time-lapse mode now records in 4K with Dolby Vision HDR, and Audio Mix can separate music from background noise. For filmmakers, both phones support 4K 120fps Dolby Vision recording, ProRes RAW, Apple Log 2 and genlock for syncing multiple cameras.Built on a 2-nanometre process, the A20 Pro uses a 6-core CPU with two super cores and four efficiency cores. Its 7-core GPU is up to 40% faster than the A19 Pro's, according to Apple. The Dual 16-core Neural Engine has 32 cores in total, giving the chip twice the AI compute of last year's model, and memory bandwidth is up 50%. Both phones also get Apple's C2 modem, which the company says improves cellular reliability while using 15% less energy.Apple has borrowed from its M-series Mac chips for the A20 Pro's packaging. The silicon die now sits beside the memory, which takes the memory out of the heat path and lets the chip attach directly to the vapour chamber. The chamber has three times the surface area of the one in the iPhone 17 Pro and uses new materials. Apple claims up to 40% better sustained performance, so demanding games and larger on-device AI models can run for longer.The Indian iPhone 18 Pro Max gets up to 43 hours of video playback and up to 29 hours of typical use on a charge, according to Apple. The iPhone 18 Pro gets up to 34 hours of video playback. eSIM-only models sold in the US and some other markets get two extra hours. Wired charging reaches 50% in around 15 minutes on both phones, but only with a 60W adapter that supports Adjustable Voltage Supply, sold separately.New display technology lets Apple shrink the Dynamic Island while keeping Face ID inside it, and it can now show three Live Activities together. The displays stay at 6.3 and 6.9 inches, with ProMotion up to 120Hz. Both phones use an aluminium unibody with Ceramic Shield 2 on the front and an IP68 rating. The Pro weighs 211g and the Pro Max 249g. Apple's EU repairability filing rates both class C, with a score of 3.14 against 3.04 for the iPhone 17 Pro models.iOS 27 rolls out on September 14, bringing Siri AI in beta. The new assistant can find information across messages, emails and photos, take action on what is on screen, and answer questions using online information. It can also draft text in the user's own writing style in Messages and Mail, while a Siri mode in the Camera app answers questions about what is in front of the lens. Siri AI starts in English, with French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish coming in October.Features that run on Apple's servers, including Siri AI, come with daily usage limits, and Apple says expanded access will cost extra in the future.
Article Summary: iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max come in four storage variants, starting at 256GB. The new Pro models also get the 2nm A20 Pro chip, a larger vapour chamber, longer battery life, a smaller Dynamic Island and Siri AI, Apple's all- new assistant that arrives with iOS 27.

Article Title: PayU launches Agent HQ, an AI agent store for SMB merchants
Article Text: PayU has announced Agent HQ, a dedicated AI agent store designed for Indian SMB merchants. The platform allows businesses to deploy specialised AI agents for every stage of commerce—from improving discoverability on AI shopping platforms to simplifying daily payment operations and powering custom conversational AI experiences.With nearly 50% of search traffic shifting to AI agents and AI‑referred shoppers converting up to three times better, PayU aims to give SMBs a level playing field. Agent HQ is built on more than a decade of commerce intelligence across 4.5 lakh+ merchants, 700+ million shopper journeys, and Rs 7,800 billion in processed transactions.Through Agent HQ, merchants can make their products and services discoverable and transactable on AI platforms like Claude, ChatGPT, and channels such as WhatsApp. They can also build custom conversational AI assistants for websites, apps and customer journeys, enabling real‑time shopper support and post‑purchase query handling.Agent HQ offers AI agents that automate operational tasks such as transaction follow‑ups, chargeback reconciliations, refund escalations and settlements. Using merchant transaction data—including success/failure patterns, chargeback histories and shopper behaviour—these agents can also suggest targeted campaigns across sales and marketing, helping reduce fraud, disputes and operational effort.Agent HQ is built directly into the PayU merchant dashboard. Merchants can hire an AI agent in a few clicks, set its frequency, monitor activity, and receive outputs via email and WhatsApp. All agents operate strictly within merchant‑defined boundaries.Manas Mishra, Chief Product Officer, PayU & Wibmo, said Agent HQ expands PayU’s value‑added offerings by giving merchants a personalised team of AI agents to improve discoverability, drive growth and manage payment operations.Merchants including Policybazaar, Daily Objects, and Pinq Polka are already using Agent HQ to enhance their commerce workflows.
Article Summary: PayU has announced Agent HQ, a dedicated AI agent store for Indian SMB merchants. The platform allows businesses to deploy specialised AI agents for every stage of commerce. Article Title: Apple Watch Ultra 4: First impressions
Article Text:
Design

Display

Features and performance

What we think

Apple Watch Ultra 4 doesn't change what the Ultra line looks like on your wrist, but it changes what it knows about you while it's there. Apple has refreshed its Watch Ultra lineup with the launch of all new Apple Watch Ultra 4 at the company’s ’Surprise Shine’ event on September 9. Successor to the Apple Watch Ultra 3, the Ultra 4 feature new Health Sensing System, which claims to provide the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable, powerful insights including readiness and longer battery life. We had the chance to spend some time with the Apple Watch Ultra 4, and here are our initial impressions of Apple’s latest rugged wearable.Apple Watch Ultra 4 keeps the rugged, unmistakable Ultra silhouette, available in the same natural and black titanium finishes as before. It's a design Apple has clearly settled on as the right one for its most durable watch, and there's no attempt to reinvent it here — the case still feels substantial on the wrist without tipping into cumbersome, and the titanium build continues to feel like it's genuinely built for the outdoors rather than just styled to look like it.The band lineup gets a proper refresh this year. Trail Loop adds dark umber, sand, and burgundy options, while Alpine Loop picks up desert, dark olive, and burgundy.The most interesting material change is on the Ocean Band, now made from a unique translucent silicone available in translucent gray, translucent kelp, and translucent black — a genuinely different look from the solid-colour bands Apple has offered in the past, and one that feels distinctly suited to the Ultra's adventure-sport identity. For Hermès buyers, the collection adds a striking new Grand H titanium band with a built-in extension mechanism that lets it stretch to fit over a wet suit — a small but thoughtful detail for anyone actually using the watch the way Apple markets it.Apple didn't make display technology the headline story with Ultra 4, and that continues a trend from recent Ultra generations — the large, bright, titanium-wrapped display that's made the Ultra legible in direct sunlight and usable with gloves on remains the foundation here. Where the display does become more useful this year is through software: a new heart rate watch face complication surfaces real-time heart rate data at a glance, and a new Steps complication does the same for step count, both readable instantly without opening a separate app. The Smart Stack also becomes more capable, with contextual suggestions — like a parked-car reminder from Maps — surfacing directly on screen, plus a new single-handed tap gesture for selecting individual widgets without needing a free hand.This is where Apple Watch Ultra 4 makes its real case for an upgrade. At the core is Apple's new Health Sensing System paired with the S11 chip, which Apple says delivers the most accurate heart rate sensing of any wearable currently available — validated in a study spanning more than 1,000 participants against competing devices. In daily use, the most noticeable change is frequency: heart rate is now measured every five seconds, all day long, and heart rate variability is tracked up to 24 times more often than before, split into recovery HRV for day-to-day stress signals and overall HRV for broader cardiovascular insight.That denser data stream feeds directly into readiness, the watch's headline new feature. Each day, Ultra 4 combines recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep score into a single 0-10 score paired with a clear recommendation — Recover, Pace Yourself, Ready, or Go For It — and it updates in real time as new data comes in, whether that's from an intense workout or a shift in daytime vitals. For an audience of athletes and endurance competitors, having that kind of daily gut-check feels like a genuinely practical addition rather than just another number to track.Battery life sees a substantial jump. Everyday use now stretches to up to 50 hours, and Low Power Mode extends that to as much as 84 hours — genuinely multi-day territory for a device this capable. Charging is also faster, with just 15 minutes on the charger adding up to 18 hours of battery back. For outdoor athletes specifically, the new Extended Workout mode delivers up to 25 hours of tracking with full GPS and heart rate data, a 25% jump over the previous model, while the new Max Extended Workout mode stretches that to 45 hours — enough, Apple notes, to track a full 100-mile race while still logging GPS readings every second. Step tracking has also been overhauled with new machine learning models, and Apple now claims it as the most accurate step tracking of any smartwatch, alongside claiming the most accurate on-device GPS in a sports watch.The most forward-looking additions are the new Audio Intelligence features arriving later this year. Live Rewind lets you double-press the Digital Crown to instantly pull up the last 15 seconds of a conversation as text — genuinely useful mid-run or mid-hike when you half-catch something a training partner said. Siri Recap goes further, generating a title and key points from a conversation afterward for later review, and Sound Recognition extends accessibility features to the wrist, alerting users who are deaf or hard of hearing to sounds like sirens or alarms even without an iPhone nearby. Apple has clearly built privacy into these features from the ground up rather than adding it as an afterthought: audio is processed in an isolated hardware compartment on the S11 chip and immediately discarded, nothing is stored as a recording, and features like Live Rewind visibly and audibly signal to people nearby when they're active.Layered on top is Siri AI, arriving with watchOS 27, bringing genuine personal context awareness to the wrist, accessible through a new Siri Modular watch face — a meaningful step up from Siri's previous, more limited capabilities on Apple Watch.Apple Watch Ultra 4 doesn't ask you to fall in love with a new shape or a flashier screen — it asks you to trust that its sensors, battery, and software have all gotten meaningfully smarter since last year, and on that front, it delivers. The jump to five-second heart rate sensing, the introduction of readiness as an actual daily decision-making tool, and battery life stretching to 45 hours of full GPS tracking for ultra-endurance events are all substantial, practical improvements for the athletes and adventurers this watch is built for. For the complete analysis on the Watch Ultra 4 you will have to wait for our detailed review.
Article Summary: Apple Watch Ultra 4 is the successor to the Apple Watch Ultra 3. New Health Sensing System claims to provide the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable. New Extended Workout mode delivers up to 25 hours of tracking with full GPS and heart rate data.

Article Title: Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigns, warns AI could ‘kill us all by the end of the decade’: ‘They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence’
Article Text:
Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon has resigned, warning that AI labs are “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence” and could potentially create systems capable of catastrophic harm. (Photo: Terminator movie still)

‘They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence ’

Jacob Coxon says current AI models do not pose an extinction risk

‘Within a year, we’ll no longer need humans’ for some research, Coxon says

AI safety concerns are growing across Silicon Valley

Anthropic and OpenAI face growing questions over AI regulation

Sam Altman says AI companies may need to slow development

Coxon calls for coordination rather than an AI race

Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon has issued a stark warning about the future of artificial intelligence, claiming that people developing advanced AI systems genuinely believe the technology could become capable of killing humanity by the end of the decade.Coxon, 27, announced his resignation from Anthropic in a series of posts on X, saying he had spent the previous three years conducting pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. He accused both companies of moving too quickly toward self-improving artificial intelligence and argued that the risks associated with increasingly autonomous AI systems are not being adequately addressed.“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” Coxon wrote. He described the warning as more than a publicity strategy, claiming that some executives and senior researchers privately express serious concerns about where the technology could be heading.His comments come amid growing debate in Silicon Valley and Washington over AI safety, regulation and the rapid development of increasingly capable AI models.In his resignation post, Coxon wrote, “I resigned from Anthropic today.I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”Coxon argued that the capabilities of AI systems are advancing rapidly across areas such as coding, mathematics and research. He warned that future systems could become capable of operating independently, gaining access to resources and potentially taking actions in the real world without direct human instruction.“Do not underestimate the power of this technology,” he wrote, warning that future AI systems could become “superhuman” in multiple domains.Coxon also raised concerns about what he described as a potential AI race between major technology companies. According to his argument, researchers at some companies may understand the risks but continue developing increasingly powerful systems because they fear competitors will move ahead if they slow down.He called entering what he described as the AI “endgame” a “hubristic gamble” and questioned whether a private company should be making decisions with potentially civilization-level consequences.Speaking to CNN after his resignation, Coxon clarified that he does not believe today's AI models are capable of causing human extinction.“Right now, there's no risk of extinction,” he said, arguing that current systems are not sufficiently intelligent to outsmart humans on the level that would be required to cause an extinction event.However, Coxon said the concern lies in the speed at which AI capabilities are improving.He pointed to recent examples of AI agents performing increasingly autonomous tasks, including alleged incidents in which AI systems interacted with or attempted to hack third-party infrastructure. Coxon argued that the significance of such developments becomes clearer when considered alongside the possibility of future systems becoming substantially more capable.“If you extrapolate into the future, considering the level of capabilities these AIs could have while retaining the same independent volition, they could cause extreme havoc,” Coxon told CNN.He cited potential threats including attacks on critical infrastructure and the creation of dangerous biological weapons as examples of how increasingly autonomous AI could potentially be misused or become difficult to control.Coxon said the pace of AI development is what changed his assessment of the technology's long-term risks.He pointed to coding and mathematics as examples, arguing that AI systems that once primarily assisted humans are increasingly capable of performing tasks independently.“A couple of years ago, these AIs were just about helping humans a little bit. They could give you suggestions. Now they're close to replacing them,” he said.While humans remain necessary for many research tasks today, Coxon suggested that could change rapidly.“Quite plausibly, within a year, we'll no longer need humans for doing research in many areas,” he told CNN.He also expressed concern about recursive self-improvement, a scenario in which increasingly capable AI systems could contribute to the development of even more capable successors, potentially accelerating technological progress beyond researchers' ability to reliably monitor or control it.Coxon’s resignation is part of a broader debate among AI researchers and employees about the potential risks of advanced artificial intelligence.In recent years, researchers and former employees at major AI companies have publicly raised concerns about the speed of development, the adequacy of safety measures and the possibility that increasingly capable systems could eventually become difficult for humans to control.In July, nearly 1,400 AI company employees reportedly signed an open letter calling for stronger government oversight of the technology. The debate has also intensified as leading AI laboratories race to develop more advanced models and autonomous agents.OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki has also warned that AI capabilities are advancing faster than researchers' ability to reliably monitor and control them.The disagreement is not necessarily over the risks posed by current AI models, but rather over what happens as systems become substantially more capable.The warnings come as the United States continues to debate how aggressively AI should be regulated.The Trump administration has moved against some state-level AI regulations, while Congress has yet to establish a comprehensive federal framework governing the development of increasingly powerful AI systems. Critics of stricter regulation have also argued that imposing heavy restrictions on US technology companies could allow China to gain an advantage in the global AI race.China, however, has introduced regulations governing aspects of artificial intelligence, including measures requiring companies to label certain AI-generated content and improve transparency and traceability.At the same time, China has not adopted the kind of sweeping restrictions that some AI-safety advocates in Silicon Valley have called for.In the US, much of the responsibility for evaluating AI safety continues to rest with the companies developing the technology.OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has himself acknowledged that the rapid advancement of AI may require a different approach to the pace of development.In July, speaking on the Invest Like The Best podcast, Altman said recent testing incidents involving advanced AI models were raising “long-term questions” about how companies should manage rapidly increasing capabilities.“We may have to pace the rate of AI development to give ourselves enough time for society to harden around these new capability levels,” Altman said.Anthropic subsequently echoed the sentiment, saying the industry could benefit from a coordinated approach to releasing increasingly powerful AI models.“We believe the world would benefit from the industry adopting a lawful, verifiable way to work together to pace how we release powerful models,” Anthropic said in a statement.Despite his warnings, Coxon said he remains optimistic that governments and AI companies could still coordinate to reduce the risks associated with advanced AI.He pointed to recent AI security incidents as potential “warning shots” that could make agreements between major US AI laboratories more achievable.However, he argued that preventing a global race may require much more significant measures, potentially including a temporary halt to improvements in model capabilities.
Article Summary: Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon has resigned, warning that AI labs are ‘racing straight to self-improving superintelligence’ Coxon says people developing advanced AI systems genuinely believe the technology could become capable of killing humanity by the end of the decade. His comments come amid growing debate in Silicon Valley and Washington over AI safety, regulation and the rapid development of increasingly capable AI models.

Article Title: Swiggy, Snowflake partner to power data-driven decisions across food, quick commerce and dining out
Article Text: Snowflake, the AI Data Cloud company, has announced that Swiggy is leveraging Snowflake as its unified data foundation. Snowflake’s platform empowers Swiggy to democratise insights across marketing and operations, enabling the company to act on customer needs in real time and accelerate business execution at scale.As Swiggy rapidly scaled to serve millions of customers across food delivery, Instamart and Dineout, getting insights from fragmented data became a challenge. The company required a unified serving layer to support peak workloads smoothly. Swiggy also sought to empower its teams with easy-to-use, self-service access to insights to reduce dependency on central data teams.“At Swiggy, data is valuable only when it reaches the person who can act on it, whether that is a city sales manager, restaurant owner or delivery partner. With Snowflake, we are making trusted, governed insights easier to access while ensuring that every user and AI agent operates within the same permissions and audit framework,” said Swiggy CTO Madhusudhan Rao.By establishing a central analytical layer on Snowflake using Apache Iceberg, Swiggy has transformed its data ecosystem. This integrated foundation enhanced Swiggy’s slowest data workflows by 90 to 96%, the companies claim.Additionally, the company improved its heaviest queries from two hours to 15 minutes and accelerated data processing from six hours to near real-time.“India's fastest-moving companies can't afford to route every data question through a central team. With Snowflake, Swiggy has built a centralised, governed data foundation, consistent controls, and an AI framework that holds agents to the same standards as people. This approach is helping Swiggy create a path toward more capable and accountable AI agents,” added Vijayant Rai, Managing Director- India, Snowflake.These performance gains have accelerated Swiggy’s daily execution across departments. Marketing teams now build and launch targeted campaigns directly within their own tools. Product engineering teams rely on standardised metric definitions to evaluate experimental features before release, using an in-house platform running directly on Snowflake.Operational teams monitor service quality metrics in real time, helping proactively improve delivery logistics. At the same time, finance teams gain workload-level visibility into technology expenses.Throughout the business, security features like role-based access, column masking, and row-level security enable both internal teams and external partners to interact with data safely using masked data. Snowflake’s governance framework further helps ensure that AI-powered agents and applications inherit the same permission boundaries, short-lived credentials, and audit trails required of human employees.
Article Summary: Swiggy is leveraging Snowflake as its unified data foundation. Snowflake’s platform empowers Swiggy to democratise insights across marketing and operations. This enables the company to act on customer needs in real time and accelerate business execution at scale.

Article Title: Google reveals massive surges for Matcha, Ube and Hojicha in India
Article Text:
Health and functional queries also climb

While search interest for matcha peaked in mid-2025, curiosity remains high. People are searching for fun combinations and at-home kits, while first-timers ask “what does matcha taste like.”

Seasonal favourites: Summer saw searches spike for “mango matcha” (+200%) and “strawberry matcha” (+400%), while the monsoon triggered breakout interest in “dirty matcha” and “coconut matcha”.

Matcha has entered our kitchens: In addition to the 1300% surge for “how to make matcha”, “matcha whisk” and “matcha bowl” became breakout searches in August 2026.

Functional wellness: Searches for “matcha health” are up 1000% and “matcha protein” is up 2500%. People are also evaluating caffeine levels, pushing “does matcha have caffeine” up 70% and “matcha vs coffee” to breakout status.

The lifestyle crossover: Searches for “matcha shoes” and “matcha enzyme scrub” emerged as breakout queries over the past year, while August 2026 saw surges for “matcha candle”, “matcha face wash”, and “matcha perfume.”

The rise of Ube and Roasted Hōjicha on Google Search

India’s cafe counters and home kitchens are seeing a wave of experimental drink choices, and that is reflected on Google Search. According to the company, Indian consumers are leaning heavily into specialised flavors like Matcha, sweet purple yam (Ube), and roasted Japanese green tea (Hōjicha). While broad search queries for matcha reached their initial high point in mid-2025, interest across Indian households continues to accelerate. Inquiries for “how to make matcha” jumped 1300% over the past twelve months, with specialised accessories like the “matcha whisk” and “matcha bowl” turning into breakout search queries in August 2026.According to the data Google collected, warmer summer weather pushed lookups for “mango matcha” up 200% and “strawberry matcha” up 400%, followed by rainy-season spikes for combinations like “coconut matcha” and “dirty matcha.”Queries around wellness considerations increased with questions around “matcha health” climbed 1000%, while “matcha protein” leaped 2500%. Buyers also examined stimulant levels, lifting questions around “does matcha have caffeine” by 70% alongside breakout growth for “matcha vs coffee.”The green tea trend has crossed into lifestyle commerce, sparking breakout queries over the year for items like “matcha enzyme scrub” and “matcha shoes,” alongside August 2026 spikes for candles, facial washes, and perfumes infused with the ingredient.Alongside matcha, two emerging flavors are posting record search volumes in India. The first is Purple Yam Wave as lookups for Ube hit an all-time peak in August 2026. Experimental drinkers drove breakout attention for fusion beverages like “ube matcha” and “ube coconut,” alongside climbs for “ube latte” and “ube cafe.”The second is Hōjicha's roasted profile as searches for Japanese roasted green tea reached an all-time ceiling in March 2026 before witnessing another breakout spike in August 2026, with users exploring “what is hojicha,” ordering “hojicha latte,” and driving breakout growth for the direct comparison “hojicha vs matcha.”Telangana leads nationwide curiosity for Ube, Delhi acts as the primary hub for Hōjicha interest, while Delhi, Chandigarh, and Goa take the top spots for residents querying “matcha near me.”
Article Summary: Search interest for matcha peaked in mid-2025, but curiosity remains high. Summer saw searches spike for “mango matcha” and “strawberry matcha,” followed by rainy-season spikes for combinations like “coconut matcha.” Indian consumers are leaning heavily into specialised flavors like Matcha, sweet purple yam, and roasted Japanese green tea (Hōjicha)

Article Title: Why iPhones are so expensive in India, again
Article Text:
We all know what’s to blame.

India was an expensive place to buy an iPhone, until it wasn't

A good part of this has nothing to do with Apple

The rest of it is a decision Apple made

Wanting one, and affording one

The best time to buy a new iPhone was yesterday. That's been the going wisdom for years, and today it's just a statement of fact. Apple's first foldable, the iPhone Duo, lands in India at Rs 2,99,900. The iPhone 18 Pro starts at Rs 1,64,900. Can’t exactly say nobody was surprised. But new phones get new prices, and we'd been told for months that this year's would sting.The older iPhones getting pricier wasn't a surprise, even though it broke from how this usually works. Prices don't normally move once a phone's already on shelves for a year, it rather go down. But Tim Cook had already said as much. Nobody was caught off guard when it landed. The iPhone 17 launched last year at Rs 82,900 and it's Rs 99,900 now. The 17e went up from Rs 64,900 to Rs 79,900. The Air was Rs 1,19,900 and it's Rs 1,49,900. Nothing about either phone changed overnight except the price.What nobody had priced in was how much of that increase would land here. Older iPhones in the US went up by a flat $100. The same phones in India went up by two and three times that.Some of it is cost. Some of it is a decision. Telling the two apart is worth doing here, because the difference matters more here than it would anywhere else.India didn't get the first iPhone at all. The 2007 model never launched here. What we got, in 2008, was the iPhone 3G at Rs 31,000, about three times what an American was paying for the same handset.Ten years on, not much had changed. The iPhone X came in at Rs 89,000 in 2017 while the US paid $999, which worked out to something near Rs 64,000 at the time. A quarter of the Indian price was tax, duty and the cost of getting the box into the country. Duty went up twice in those years. If you wanted an iPhone you got it at duty free, or you asked a cousin flying back from Dubai, or you didn't get one.Then Apple started building them here and the maths changed. First the SE, then the vanilla models, until Pros were rolling out within weeks of a Cupertino launch. The base price stopped climbing. The iPhone 12 launched at Rs 79,900 in 2020, and so did the 13, the 14, the 15 and the 16. The Pros were being priced with some restraint too. The 16 Pro actually launched below the 15 Pro, at Rs 1,19,900. The 16e came in under all of them at Rs 59,900. The stores opened in Mumbai and Delhi. No cost EMI turned Rs 79,900 into a monthly number many never thought twice about.Five years of that, and the iPhone stopped being something many saved up for. It worked, too. India moved into Apple's top handful of markets by shipments, the sort of place the company started naming on earnings calls instead of grouping into "rest of world".Apple's position here is secure enough. What moved this week were the prices underneath it. The cheapest new iPhone you can buy today is Rs 20,000 above where the entry model sat eighteen months ago, and the 17e alone is up Rs 15,000 since March. It isn't even six months old yet.A fair bit of the gap is just tax and duty. Tarun Pathak, research director at Counterpoint Research, breaks the Duo's India price into a stack. Around 17 percent import duty. Another 18 percent GST. By his estimate, a further 5 to 6 percent from currency movement. That's past 40 percent before Apple has decided anything about margin, and the Duo takes the full hit, because it won't be assembled here for a while and lands as a finished import.That's how a $1,999 phone reaches you at Rs 2,99,900, and Rs 4,49,900 if you want the 2TB one. It's also why the iPhones made here sit much closer to their dollar price. The 17 Pro was $1,099 in the US and Rs 1,34,900 here. The 18 Pro is $1,199 and Rs 1,64,900. Those are gaps you can at least follow. The Duo's is nothing like it.That stack also explains why a dollar increase never arrives here as a dollar increase. Duty and GST are percentages, so they scale with whatever Apple adds at the top. A $100 rise is roughly Rs 8,800 to begin with, and by the time GST has been applied, and duty too if the phone is imported, it reaches a shelf here at somewhere between Rs 10,000 and Rs 12,000. Every cost increase Apple absorbs globally gets amplified on the way into this market, and this year there were a lot of them.None of that is new, though. The same stack was in place last year, and last year it still put the iPhone 17 on shelves at Rs 82,900.Taxes explains the level, what it doesn't explain is the jump.What moved is the memory, and Apple did warn us. Back in June, Tim Cook sat down for an interview with one purpose: to say that price rises were coming and couldn't be avoided. He wouldn't say which products or by how much. He called what's happening to memory a hundred-year flood, and said that in forty years around the electronics supply chain he'd never seen anything like it. People took the hint. The advice going around ever since has been to buy whatever Apple product you were planning to buy, immediately.He was talking about memory, which covers two things on a spec sheet. The RAM a phone runs on and the storage it fills up. Both used to get cheaper every cycle, reliably, for four decades. That's stopped. Supply chain estimates put 16GB of smartphone DRAM at roughly $42 in mid 2025 and roughly $181 a year later. Those are dollar figures, and they stay dollar figures no matter where the phone is eventually put together.The reason is AI, which by now you could have guessed.The three companies that make almost all the world's memory also make the high-bandwidth memory that AI servers run on, and that business pays better, ships in bigger volumes and comes with multiyear contracts. Apple used to have enough leverage to squeeze those suppliers down to almost nothing. Now it waits in line like everybody else. Ternus spent yesterday's keynote arguing that the iPhone is already the best AI device anybody has built, and the same AI is why it costs what it does.Everyone is passing it on. The Pixel 11 came in at $899 against $799 for the Pixel 10, and at Rs 89,999 here, with every model in the family costing more than the Pixel 10 it replaced. Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra sits at about Rs 2 lakh and the Fold 8 at Rs 1,79,999, the most Samsung has ever charged for a foldable in India. Anything with a chip in it has been getting dearer all year: laptops, consoles, cars, the lot. Apple was late to it the way it was late to foldables, and it won't be early to the recovery either. Memory fabs take years to build, and most forecasts don't have supply catching demand before late 2027.Run that multiplier on the iPhone 17 and you get to about Rs 12,000. The price went up by Rs 17,000. On the Air it went up by Rs 30,000. Tax and duty do not get you there.There's a pattern in how the increases were applied, too. In the US every older model went up by the same $100, which works out to 10 percent on the Air and closer to 17 percent on the 17e. Here the increases were far more even in percentage terms, roughly 20 to 25 percent on each of the 17, the 17e and the Air, whatever the phone cost to begin with. A component shock lands as a fixed cost per device. What was applied here looks more like the whole ladder being reset.The Air is where that shows up worst. It was always a slightly strange buy, a thin phone with one camera at Rs 1,19,900, sold on how it felt rather than what it did. At Rs 1,49,900 it now sits Rs 15,000 under a current generation iPhone 18 Pro. In the US the same two phones are $100 apart on a much bigger base. The middle of the range here hasn't just moved up, it has been squeezed flat.Prabhu Ram, who heads the industry research group at CyberMedia Research, puts the rest down to a list of things that have nothing to do with components: the rupee, local tax structure, channel economics, and Apple's own reading of what India's affluent buyers are willing to spend. The channel part matters more here than most people assume. Apple sells the bulk of its phones in the US directly. Here it moves through distributors, large format retail and thousands of smaller stores, and every one of those margins sits inside the price on the sticker.Then there's the last variable, which is Apple's judgement. It has never converted its American price and printed the sticker. It prices each market on what it thinks that market will pay, and it has seemingly decided we'll pay quite a lot.None of this works without the financing, though. The Duo comes to about Rs 48,800 a month across six no-cost instalments and the 18 Pro to about Rs 26,300, and the monthly figure is what the people buying these phones actually respond to. It also means the Rs 30,000 that went onto the Air reaches a buyer as Rs 5,000 a month, which is far easier to absorb than it looks on a price list.The aspirational class explanation is one you'll have heard for a decade now, and it keeps being the right one. India's aspirational class, the way Ram reads it, is still confident about discretionary spending, particularly on things that work as premium lifestyle statements. That gives Apple room at the top of the range it doesn't have in most markets.The lineup shows it better than any single price does. The Duo isn't here to sell in volume. It sits above the Pro Max as a new ultra premium tier, a halo that lifts the average selling price of everything below it, and Pathak expects it to grow India's foldable segment by value long before it does by volume. The Pro line has taken a 20 to 22 percent increase, and that's where the memory cost is actually being passed on.Then there's what Apple hasn't done. There's no standard iPhone 18 this year. That phone, the 18e and a second Air are all expected around March. The base iPhone 17 went up instead of coming down the way last year's model always does. So the usual move, buying the previous phone at a discount, isn't on the table until spring. Anyone who would have made that move and still wants a current iPhone gets pointed at the Pro, and the Pro is what lifts the average.None of which means Apple sells less here in rupee terms. Pathak expects volumes to slip while revenue keeps climbing, a low single digit decline in units against 6 to 7 percent growth in value. The mix does it. Apple grew 2 percent year on year between January and July, the Pro series grew 32 percent over the same stretch, and Pro's share of Apple's India sales is on track to go from 11 percent last year to about 15 percent by the end of this one.A lot rides on the festive quarter now, on trade-in schemes and on older iPhones continuing to sell, the iPhone 15 included. Pathak also sees the refurbished market growing faster than anyone had planned for, and that's hard to argue with. Every buyer pushed up the ladder leaves a phone behind.That is also the quiet reason increases keep getting absorbed here. An iPhone holds its value better than anything else sold in this market, so what a buyer actually pays over two or three years has never risen as fast as the sticker suggests. A Rs 99,900 phone that fetches half of that on trade-in is a different proposition from a Rs 99,900 phone that fetches a quarter.There's even a case that Apple comes out of this ahead of its rivals, because budget and mid-range Android makers have nowhere near the margin to absorb a shock like this one. Their prices have gone up too, and some of the cheapest models have stopped being made at all. When the phone you bought because it was cheap isn't cheap anymore, an iPhone stops looking so far away.For people who aspire to own Apple's newest hardware, and it has become a strong aspiration again, the question is turning into how to keep an iPhone within reach at all. You hold on to one longer. You trade it in. You buy refurbished, you wait for the sales or you stretch the payments out. None of it makes the phone any cheaper.And none of it can be fixed at this end either. Building phones in India closed the distance between the American price and ours, and it did that job well for five years. But a phone assembled here is still full of imported parts bought in dollars, so when the cost moved from the shipping container to the inside of the device, the advantage this market spent a decade building simply didn't apply.Apple can still earn more from India while selling fewer phones, but that is a different growth story from bringing more Indians into its ecosystem. The festive season will show how much room is left between wanting an iPhone and being able to afford one. Discounts and instalments can soften the price of admission. They can't disguise how much higher the entry fee has been set.
Article Summary: Apple's first foldable, the iPhone Duo, lands in India at Rs 2,99,900. The iPhone 18 Pro starts at Rs 1,64,900 and the 17e at Rs 79,000. The cheapest new iPhone you can buy today is Rs 20,000 above where the entry model sat eighteen months ago. A quarter of the Indian price was tax, duty and the cost of getting the box into the country.

Article Title: Apple iPhone Duo: First impressions
Article Text:
iPhone Duo design

iPhone Duo display

iPhone Duo performance

iPhone Duo camera

What We Think

Apple iPhone Duo is finally here. Apple officially entered the foldable phone category with the launch of its first foldable smartphone – iPhone Duo at the company ‘Surprise and Shine’ event. The first foldable smartphone from Apple, when opened, is the thinnest iPhone ever and sports a 7.6-inch inner display. It comes with an advanced camera system and the reworked iOS 27 for foldable form factor. And with Apple Intelligence and Siri AI, iPhone Duo brings powerful AI capabilities together with personal context. We had the chance to experience Apple’s first foldable smartphone, and here are our initial impressions.The first thing you notice about the iPhone Duo is just how solid it feels. Built from grade 5 titanium with a mirror-polished finish, the device carries real heft without feeling clunky, and the hinge – engineered from more than 100 individual components – snaps open and closes with a satisfying, precise feel and it doesn't wobble or feel loose in hand. A 3D-printed hinge cover with a contrasting micro-blasted finish adds a nice visual detail against the mirrored body, and an integrated magnet array pulls the two halves shut with a clean, secure closure.Talking about durability, Ceramic Shield protects the back and with a new Ceramic Shield 2 on the front display, Apple claims three times better scratch resistance than the outgoing generation. The foldable smartphone from Apple comes with IP68 rating which makes it resistant to splash, dust and water. Internally, support ribs and ceramic fiber antenna inserts reinforce the frame, and it shows: there's none of the flex or creak you sometimes feel in early-generation foldables.Open, iPhone Duo is described as the thinnest iPhone ever made, and it genuinely feels that way in hand. The smartphone is slim enough that unfolding it doesn't feel like unpacking a small tablet. Closed, it's compact enough to operate comfortably one-handed and drops into a pocket without the awkward bulk some foldables carry. The button placement is also done thoughtfully, the power button sits on the right side which also doubles up as the Touch ID. The volume control button is now located at the top making it easier for the user to access in all the different modes. In all, the iPhone Duo will impress you with its slim and sleek design.Apple's approach to the dual-screen setup on iPhone Duo is refreshingly cohesive rather than feeling like two separate devices bolted together. The foldable phone houses a 5.4-inch Super Retina XDR display with 1398×2034 pixel resolution. The vibrant outer display offers plenty of room for routine tasks such as messaging, checking notifications, or quickly snapping a photo without needing to unfold the phone at all. On the other hand, once you unfold the device you will find the 7.6-inch inner display with 1878×2670 pixel resolution. In practice, it transforms the phone into a compact tablet, and the shared aspect ratio between the two displays means content resizes cleanly when you fold or unfold the device rather than awkwardly cropping or stretching.Apple has incorporated nano-texture finish on the internal display. This is a smart move of the company as it helps in cutting down the glare and gives a soft and matte feel to the display. Along with this, the nano-texture finish also works well in disguising the crease along the fold, a detail that has plagued rival foldables for years. Both the screens on the iPhone Duo support ProMotion, Always-On and Apple’s stated peak outdoor brightness of 3000 nits, so brightness and smoothness don't feel like a compromise on either screen. The FaceTime camera is also hidden beneath the inner display keeping the screen visually uninterrupted rather than relying on a notch or punch-hole cutout.Under the hood, iPhone Duo runs on the same A20 Pro chip found in the iPhone 18 Pro lineup, built on a 2-nanometer process and paired with a custom vapour chamber cooling system inspired by Apple's M-series chip packaging. Apple claims up to 35% better sustained performance compared to the iPhone 17 Pro, and in short bursts of multitasking and app-switching during our time with the device, everything felt immediate — no visible lag when snapping between split-screen apps or reopening the device from standby.Software is where iPhone Duo genuinely differentiates itself from simply being a big-screen iPhone. iOS 27 has been meaningfully reworked for the form factor: navigation elements shift to the side of the screen to maximize vertical space, the Dynamic Island adapts to sit vertically along the edge of either display, and Split View finally brings true side-by-side multitasking to iPhone for the first time, letting two full apps run simultaneously, or two windows of the same app for quick comparisons.Apple Intelligence and the newly-overhauled Siri AI are also front and center, with the assistant now capable of drawing on personal context across messages, photos, and email, and taking action based on whatever's on-screen. Being able to keep a conversation running with Siri on one side of the inner display while working in another app on the other side felt like a genuinely new way to use a phone, not just a bigger version of an old one. Third-party apps like Slack, Zoom, and Netflix have already been rebuilt to take advantage of the larger canvas, and it shows – Zoom in particular turns the inner display into something closer to a small conference room view than a typical phone call.The rear camera system carries over familiar high-end iPhone hardware — a 48MP Fusion Main camera with an integrated optical-quality 2x telephoto, and a 48MP Fusion Ultra Wide lens matching the one found on iPhone 18 Pro models — but the folding design is what makes the camera experience here feel genuinely new rather than just another spec bump.Being able to prop the phone up using its own hinge and use the outer display as a live viewfinder (a feature Apple calls Duo Preview) makes self-portraits and group shots noticeably easier to frame without needing a tripod or a helping hand. A feature called Smart Take, which uses on-device AI to automatically fire the shutter when it detects everyone in frame is actually posing, solved the age-old problem of just missing the moment while still setting up the shot. There's also Duo FaceTime, which lets someone standing next to you join a video call through the outer display without everyone needing to crowd around one screen — a small but genuinely clever use of the second display during testing.Video capabilities are equally strong on paper, with 4K120fps Dolby Vision recording, post-capture Cinematic effects up to 60fps, and an upgraded Audio Mix system that can now isolate music from surrounding voices. None of these are entirely new tricks for iPhone, but the ability to prop the device up hands-free for longer recording sessions, thanks to the built-in hinge, adds real practical value.iPhone Duo doesn't feel like a proof-of-concept the way early foldables from other manufacturers often did. The hinge feels genuinely durable rather than a stated concern, the display crease is about as well-disguised as we've seen in the category so far, and the software rework in iOS 27 makes a real case for why a second, larger screen actually changes how you use the phone rather than just making everything bigger. Between Split View multitasking, the reworked Siri AI experience, and folding-specific camera tricks like Duo Preview and Smart Take, Apple has clearly spent time thinking through what a foldable iPhone should feel like to actually live with, rather than rushing out a first-generation device to check a box. But as a first impression, iPhone Duo feels like a genuinely considered debut rather than an experiment – one that positions Apple to compete seriously in the foldable category it waited the longest to enter.
Article Summary: iPhone Duo is the first foldable smartphone from Apple. When opened, it is the thinnest iPhone ever and sports a 7.6-inch inner display. It comes with an advanced camera system and the reworked iOS 27 for foldable form factor. It also comes with Apple Intelligence and Siri AI.

NEW DELHI: The rush to replace workers and give artificial intelligence access to critical systems could cause serious harm without machines ever surpassing human intelligence, a University of Surrey expert has warned, as an industry resignation renews calls for international oversight.Andrew Rogoyski, from the university’s Institute for People-Centred AI, said the practical dangers were premature job losses and cyber disruption, even as he questioned predictions of an imminent technological takeover.His comments follow Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon’s resignation on September 8. Coxon accused the company and OpenAI of racing irresponsibly towards self-improving superintelligence. British MP Darren Jones has called for a multinational treaty governing its safe development.Anthropic has said it recognises unprecedented risks and supports lawful, verifiable industry cooperation to pace the release of powerful models.“We’re right to worry about the theoretical dangers of Artificial Superintelligence (ASI), but I still believe that we are a long way from achieving this,” Rogoyski said.ASI refers to hypothetical systems far exceeding human abilities across different fields.He argued that AI remained dependent on people for electricity, cooling and computing chips. More concerning, he said, were less capable systems pursuing narrow goals while being allowed to act independently and access critical infrastructure.“In economic terms, the danger is that companies displace human workers far too early, long before AI has really proved its worth.”Rogoyski also questioned claims that one person could run a billion-dollar company using AI, arguing that technical capability alone would not make such businesses economically or socially workable.He suggested a major AI-enabled cyber attack could disrupt organisations, trigger lawsuits and drive investors away, forcing developers to prioritise safety.He also questioned whether today’s advanced AI could justify its computing and energy costs, warning of “the great disappointment” if costs remained high and usefulness fell short.He saw greater value in specialised AI with clearer benefits relative to costs.“The great shame in all this furore will be the backlash that slows down AI development in areas where it could really make a very positive difference, like curing cancer or solving climate change,” he said.
Article Summary: Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon’s resignation renews concerns over AI safety and the risks of unchecked development. British MP Darren Jones has called for a multinational treaty governing its safe development. Andrew Rogoyski, from the University of Surrey, said the practical dangers were premature job losses and cyber disruption.

Article Title: 22-year-old school dropout pleads guilty in America's largest Bitcoin robbery, posed as Google and Gemini executives; spent millions on sports cars, night clubs and mansions
Article Text:

22-year-old school dropout pleads guilty in $240 million Bitcoin theft

How a missed IP address helped investigators trace the stolen Bitcoin

“Oh, my God! Bro, bro, I’m going to spaz out!”

Sports cars, mansions and a $569,000 nightclub bill

FBI arrests after month of lavish spending

“We always talked about what it would be like if I were to go down, but never thought it would be this crazy.”

“I could only think of Ferris Bueller gone bad,”

18 defendants charged as investigation continues

“got obsessed with the image of success rather than actually becoming a hard-working individual myself.”

“Being young only goes so far,”

“If we don’t seriously ramp up the resources to take these people down and do it faster, then it’s going to spread more and more,”

A cryptocurrency investor in Washington, DC, lost more than $240 million in Bitcoin in 2024. The incident took place after a group of young scammers allegedly posed as Google and Gemini executives. Malone Lam, a 22-year-old Singaporean eighth-grade dropout accused of organising the scheme, has pleaded guilty to his role in the theft.An AP report claims that after obtaining more than 4,100 Bitcoin, Lam and his associates allegedly spent the proceeds on fleets of sports cars, private jets, rented mansions, luxury watches and nightclub outings, with Lam spending more than $569,000 at a Los Angeles nightclub in a single evening.Lam, an eighth-grade dropout from Singapore, pleaded guilty to a racketeering conspiracy charge in federal court in Washington, DC. His guilty plea makes him the 11th of 18 defendants charged in the wider investigation to plead guilty, according to prosecutors. The case centers on a network of young men who allegedly used social engineering to manipulate victims into handing over information or access to steal cryptocurrency.The theft at the center of the case took place on August 18, 2024. Prosecutors say Lam, Veer Chetal and Jeandiel Serrano targeted a wealthy, longtime cryptocurrency investor in Washington, DC.The callers allegedly first posed as a Google representative investigating attempted breaches of the victim's account, then as representatives of the Gemini cryptocurrency exchange warning about a malware attack affecting his crypto wallet.The victim was manipulated into providing access to his Google Drive and revealing security codes. Those details allegedly gave Lam the access needed to transfer more than 4,100 Bitcoin. The cryptocurrency was worth more than $240 million at the time, making the theft one of the largest cryptocurrency thefts in US history.The conspirators then allegedly used money laundering specialists and multiple cryptocurrency exchanges to move the stolen assets and convert them into government-issued currency. Prosecutors say the group had already carried out other multimillion-dollar cryptocurrency thefts using similar methods after meeting through online gaming forums in late 2023.The group attempted to conceal its digital trail, but investigators eventually found a link through Serrano. Prosecutors say he failed to hide his IP address when he created an account on a cryptocurrency exchange to hold nearly $30 million in stolen cryptocurrency.Investigators traced the IP address to a home in Encino, California, that Serrano was renting for $47,500 a month. By then, Serrano was vacationing in the Maldives, while Lam and his associates were spending the proceeds in Los Angeles and Miami.A private recording later captured the group realising how much cryptocurrency they had obtained. In a video posted by cryptocurrency crime investigator ZachXBT, one voice can be heard saying,The spending that followed quickly became another part of the investigation. Authorities say Lam and his friends spent roughly $4 million at Los Angeles nightclubs in a single month, while Lam bought more than 30 vehicles, including custom Porsches, Lamborghinis and Ferraris. He also allegedly purchased a watch worth about $2 million.The stolen cryptocurrency funded a lifestyle that included private jets, security guards and rented mansions in Miami and the Hamptons. Lam also allegedly spent hundreds of thousands of dollars per night at clubs and threw handbags worth tens of thousands of dollars to women in the crowds.One of the largest individual expenses was Lam's reported $569,000 bill at a Los Angeles nightclub during a single evening. Prosecutors say the spending was part of a month-long spree that began soon after the Bitcoin theft.Chetal allegedly used some of his share to buy a Lamborghini for his parents and hid a duffel bag containing $500,000 in cash inside their washing machine. The sudden display of wealth also attracted attention within cryptocurrency scammer circles.About a week after the Bitcoin theft, several masked men allegedly abducted Chetal's parents in Danbury, Connecticut. The attackers reportedly forced the couple from their new car, beat Chetal's father with a baseball bat, put both of them into a van and bound their hands. Prosecutors say the group, which had travelled from Miami, intended to use the couple to pressure Chetal into surrendering his share of the stolen cryptocurrency. The plan failed after witnesses contacted police and the alleged carjackers were arrested.FBI raided Chetal’s apartment in Brunswick, New Jersey, on September 9, 2024, and recovered nearly $37 million in stolen cryptocurrency, the source material claimed. However, Chetal later agreed to cooperate with investigators.Prosecutors confirmed that Serrano was arrested on Sept. 18, 2024, at Los Angeles International Airport wearing a watch estimated to be worth about $500,000. He first denied any involvement but then admitted to having some of the $20 million of the Washington victim's stolen cryptocurrency.Prosecutors arrested Lam the same day at one of his Miami mansions. According to the indictment, an off-duty law enforcement officer had warned him that authorities were coming to arrest him.After his arrest, Lam was recorded speaking to associates from jail. According to the indictment, he said,At Lam's initial court appearance in Miami, prosecutors outlined the scale of his alleged spending. US Magistrate Judge Alicia Valle responded,referring to the school-skipping protagonist of the 1986 film Ferris Bueller’s Day Off.The arrests did not immediately end the flow of stolen money. Ferro, another defendant who pleaded guilty to a racketeering conspiracy charge last year, allegedly used stolen funds to pay Lam's legal expenses.The federal investigation has resulted in charges against 18 people. Lam would become the 11th defendant to plead guilty, while three of his co-conspirators have already been sentenced.US District Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly, who is presiding over Lam's case, sentenced two money launderers to about six years in prison. Prosecutors previously estimated that Lam's sentencing guidelines could recommend at least 14 years in prison upon conviction.Chetal pleaded guilty to conspiracy charges in November 2024 and is awaiting sentencing. Serrano's charges remain pending.Tucker Desmond, who pleaded guilty to destroying evidence related to the crimes of other members of the group, was sentenced to probation. At his March sentencing hearing, Desmond apologised and said heFerro declined to address the court at his May sentencing hearing. His attorney, Kevin Wilson, described the defendants as mischievousbut Judge Kollar-Kotelly rejected youth as a complete explanation for their conduct.Kollar-Kotelly said.The case also highlights the growing use of social engineering in cryptocurrency crime. Cybersecurity researcher Allison Nixon, who has tracked The Com, an underground community of young hackers, said the amount of money available through cryptocurrency fraud has helped fuel the activity.Nixon said.The broader issue has also drawn attention as cryptocurrency-related fraud complaints have increased. FBI complaints involving cryptocurrency investment fraud rose by nearly 50% in 2025, according to the source material. The Justice Department also disbanded a unit dedicated to prosecuting crypto-related crimes last year.Lam's guilty plea marks the latest step in an investigation that began with an online social network of young hackers and developed into a scheme targeting cryptocurrency holders. What started with impersonating trusted technology and financial companies ultimately led to the theft of thousands of Bitcoin, a month-long spending spree and federal charges against 18 people.
Article Summary: Malone Lam, a 22-year-old Singaporean eighth-grade dropout, has pleaded guilty to his role in the theft. Prosecutors say Lam, Veer Chetal and Jeandiel Serrano targeted a wealthy, longtime cryptocurrency investor in Washington, DC. The group allegedly used social engineering to manipulate victims into handing over information or access to steal cryptocurrency. Lam and his associates allegedly spent the proceeds on fleets of sports cars, private jets and rented mansions.

Article Title: Sandisk introduces NAS SSD portfolio in India
Article Text:
Sandisk introduces NAS SSD portfolio in India

Sandisk has launched the Sandisk NAS portfolio of high-endurance SSDs in India. Sandisk's new NAS SSD portfolio includes two high-endurance and high-performance SSDs engineered for multi-user or demanding creative professional workloads. The all-new series comprises of Sandisk NAS 600 SATA SSD and Sandisk NAS 800 NVMe SSD. In a press release, the company claims that the SSDs “are engineered to deliver the reliable, consistent performance, high-endurance, and scalability required for today's demanding NAS workloads”.Sandisk NAS 600 SATA SSD is optimized for creative professionals and small businesses modernizing NAS by replacing HDDs with SSDs or accelerating by adding a solid-state cache or tier, the Sandisk NAS 600 SATA SSD delivers high endurance with up to 2,500 TBW (4TB model) and up to 2.25M hours MTTF1 to support demanding multi-user workloads. Its 2.5”/7mm SATA form factor integrates into existing 3.5” NAS drive bays supporting 2.5” SSDs, delivering sequential reads up to 560MB/s with no mechanical noise.The SSD is available in high-endurance models from 500GB up to 4TB.Sandisk NAS 800 NVMeSSD, on the other hand, is designed for deploying all-flash and hybrid NAS running demanding or business critical workloads. The Sandisk NAS 800 NVMe SSD comes with PCIe® 5.0 is engineered with a high-endurance rating of up to 14 PBW1 (7.68TB) for caching, storage tiering, or as primary storage.It delivers up to 2.3M/2M IOPS3 random read/write speeds (3.84TB) and sequential read/write speeds up to 14,900/13,200MB/s3 (1.92TB) for multiuser collaborative environments, databases, virtualization, content creation, or agentic AI. It reliably performs in demanding NAS environments and is tested with many leading NAS systems for M.2 2280 compatibility.Users will be able to choose capacities from 960GB to 7.68TB4 with Sandisk TLC 3D NAND. Both the Sandisk NAS 600 SATA SSD and Sandisk NAS 800 NVMe SSD will be available for purchase in September at Sandisk.com, select retailers and e-tailers worldwide.Price of the Sandisk NAS 600 SATA SSD will start at $179.99 (500GB). While the Sandisk NAS 800 NVMe SSD will be available at a starting price of $309.99.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Jensen Huang: “Greatness comes from character, and character isn't formed…” - the lesson behind his powerful words
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Jensen Huang

“Greatness comes from character, and character isn't formed out of smart people — it's formed out of people who have suffered.”

Understanding the meaning behind the quote

Why Huang puts so much weight on hardship

What the quote says about resilience

Lessons from Jensen Huang's words

Intelligence has limits: Understanding a problem quickly does not always mean having the resilience to stay with it longest.

Expectations must allow for reality: High expectations can exist alongside low resilience. When results fall short, the ability to adapt matters.

Failure can provide useful information: A mistake does not define someone's ability. It can show what needs to change when examined honestly.

Patience matters: Important technological developments can take years to reveal their full impact. Nvidia's early focus on graphics eventually connected with much broader computing needs.

Success is often measured in visible things: a degree, a promotion, a company that survives, or an invention that changes an industry. Jensen Huang has spent much of his career around those measures. As the co-founder and chief executive of Nvidia, he helped take a graphics-chip company founded in 1993 into one of the most important technology companies in the world. Yet when Huang was asked about what helps people become successful, he did not point first to intelligence or academic achievement. He spoke about hardship, resilience and the way difficult experiences can shape a person. His view is summed up in a line that puts character ahead of raw ability.Huang made the remark while speaking to students at Stanford University in 2024.The distinction Huang makes is between being capable and being able to withstand difficult circumstances. Intelligence can help someone understand a complicated problem. Education can provide knowledge.Technical skill can make it possible to build something that others cannot. None of those qualities, by themselves, guarantee that a person will keep going when a plan fails or when a long period of uncertainty arrives. It is reflected in how someone behaves when circumstances become uncomfortable. A person may have to accept criticism, recover from a mistake, work through disappointment or continue making decisions without knowing whether the outcome will be favourable.Huang's argument is not that suffering automatically produces a good character. Difficult experiences can affect people in many different ways. His point is that hardship can provide situations in which resilience, patience and judgement have to be developed rather than simply understood in theory.Huang has often spoken about the difficult parts of building a company. Nvidia was founded in 1993 by Huang, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, initially with a focus on computer graphics. The company later developed the GPU, with the GeForce 256 introduced in 1999 as a landmark in the development of programmable computer graphics. Its technology eventually became central to parallel computing and artificial intelligence.That path was not simply a straight rise. Huang has described Nvidia's history as containing serious mistakes and periods when the company's future was uncertain. He has discussed several early challenges and what he described as near-death experiences for the company.This helps explain why he speaks about suffering in such practical terms. For someone who has spent decades running a technology company through changing markets, setbacks are not unusual events. They are part of the work.Resilience is easy to discuss when nothing is going wrong. It becomes more complicated when a person has invested years in something and still does not know whether it will work.Huang's comments suggest that resilience is partly built through exposure to those situations. A setback forces a person to make another decision. Failure can require an adjustment rather than an immediate answer. Repeated difficulties can also change how someone views risk, expectations and responsibility.That does not mean people should seek suffering for its own sake. Huang's comments are better understood as an observation about unavoidable hardship. Difficult experiences happen in education, careers, businesses and ordinary personal life. His argument is that avoiding every uncomfortable experience may also mean avoiding some of the situations in which resilience develops.
Article Summary: Huang made the remark while speaking to students at Stanford University in 2024. The distinction Huang makes is between being capable and being able to withstand difficult circumstances. Huang's argument is not that suffering automatically produces a good character. Difficult experiences happen in education, careers, businesses and ordinary personal life.

Apple has entered the foldable smartphone market with the iPhone Duo. Samsung, on the other hand, is already selling the Galaxy Z Fold 8 in India. The two phones use a passport-style folding design, but they differ in price, display size, cameras, processors, battery capacity and software. The iPhone Duo starts at Rs 2,99,900 in India, making it Rs 1,19,901 more expensive than the Galaxy Z Fold 8, which starts at Rs 1,79,999. Here is how the Apple iPhone Duo compares with the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 on key specifications and features.The iPhone Duo has a 7.6-inch inner display when unfolded and a 5.4-inch outer display when folded.
